title: Heartbeat + Lease
summary:
A **monitor** decides whether a **worker** is alive. The worker periodically sends a **heartbeat**; each one renews a **lease with a TTL**. If the lease expires the node is considered unreliable, and the monitor records the new state (for example in etcd) and starts recovery: requeue the node's work, remove it from routing.

**Why a lease and not "one missed heartbeat = dead"?** Heartbeats arrive late (network delay, GC, a busy NIC). The TTL is the slack. A common rule: TTL is about 3 heartbeat intervals, and renew at about TTL/3, so one or two lost or delayed beats do not cause a false death.

**Clock shift.** The monitor judges expiry on its own clock ([clock skew](#/sd/f/clock-shift)); to be safe it waits `TTL + MAX_ALLOW_CLOCK_SHIFT` before acting.

**Where heartbeats live.** Heartbeats are high-volume, low-value soft state: keep them in memory or Redis, no WAL or consensus write each time. Only *state transitions* (alive to dead) are persisted to the durable store. After a monitor restart, workers simply beat again.

**Detecting expiry efficiently.** Use a [timer wheel](#/sd/f/timer-wheel): each heartbeat cancels the worker's old timer and inserts a new one `TTL` ahead (with a *rounds* counter if the TTL spans more than one wheel revolution). When the hand reaches a bucket, scan it; timers whose rounds are 0 have expired.

**Zombie workers.** A worker may be alive but cut off (for example a congested top-of-rack switch), and still running when its work is reassigned. Defend in layers: a **grace period** before declaring death, **cancel-on-requeue** (best-effort stop of the old run), and a [fencing token](#/sd/f/fencing-token) at the resource as the guarantee. See [lease](#/sd/f/lease) and [failover](#/sd/f/failover).

drills.q: Workers heartbeat every 5 s. The lease TTL is 15 s and the monitor adds MAX_ALLOW_CLOCK_SHIFT = 2 s before declaring a node dead. A worker's last heartbeat is received at t = 100 s and the worker then crashes. At what time, in seconds, does the monitor declare it dead?
drills.explain: The lease runs to 100 + 15 = 115 s and the monitor waits the extra 2 s of clock-shift allowance, so it acts at 117 s. That is the price of avoiding false deaths: 17 s of detection delay for the 5 s interval.

drills.q: Heartbeats are sent every 5 s and the network occasionally delays one by up to 4 s. Which TTL is the best fit?
options: 5 s, equal to the interval, for the fastest detection
7 s; the delay would still have to be under 2 s
15 s, about three intervals, so one or two late or lost beats do not trigger a false failover
10 minutes, so the system never evicts healthy nodes
drills.explain: A delayed beat arrives up to 9 s after the previous one (5 + 4), which would expire a 5 s or 7 s lease even though the worker is healthy. 10 minutes makes real failures take far too long to notice.

drills.q: A worker is partitioned from the monitor, not dead. The monitor expires its lease and requeues the job to worker B; worker A, still running, tries to write the result. Which mechanism actually guarantees that A's stale write is rejected?
options: A longer grace period before declaring A dead
A shorter TTL, so A is evicted sooner
A fencing token checked by the result store, which refuses writes from the older lease generation
drills.explain: Grace periods reduce false positives, and cancel messages are best effort (A may be unreachable), but neither can stop a write that is already in flight. Only the resource itself can enforce ordering of owners.

drills.q: A fleet has 10,000 workers, each heartbeating every 5 s. How many heartbeat updates per second must the monitor absorb?
drills.explain: 10,000 / 5 s = 2,000/s, which is 7.2 million per hour. Persisting each through a replicated log would make the heartbeat path the bottleneck, so heartbeats stay in memory or Redis and only alive/dead transitions are written durably.

drills.q: Put the timer-wheel handling of one worker's lease in order.
items: A heartbeat arrives from the worker
The monitor cancels the worker's existing timer
It inserts a new timer TTL ahead into the right bucket, with a rounds counter if needed
The wheel hand reaches that bucket and scans it
A timer with rounds = 0 fires: the node is marked dead in the durable store and recovery starts
drills.explain: Cancel-and-reinsert makes each heartbeat O(1). Rounds let one wheel represent timers longer than its span: each pass decrements the counter and only a timer at 0 expires.
